title: Neutron's first launch slips again amid trouble with carbon composites
gist: Rocket Lab said its Neutron medium-lift rocket will not fly until 2027 after voids were found in carbon composite propellant domes, a defect traced to a design change made after a January tank rupture. The slip doubles the development timeline from the original 2024 target just as SpaceX shifts toward Starship.

insights.claim: Rocket Lab announced Neutron's first launch will not occur until 2027 because of a manufacturing issue in the carbon composite structures, confirming what the company and industry already knew.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: First-flight timing is the key catalyst for the Neutron thesis and has slipped again; further schedule risk remains.

insights.claim: Rocket Lab announced Neutron in 2021 aiming for a first flight in 2024, so the development timeline has now doubled.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Track record of slippage should inform skepticism of near-term dates.
insights.locator: Rocket Lab announced the Neutron rocket in 2021

insights.claim: The August update implied Rocket Lab still hoped to deliver the first Neutron to its Wallops Island, Virginia pad before year end, a schedule that would almost certainly have pushed first flight into 2027 anyway.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The 2027 date is a modest incremental slip versus the already implied schedule, not a surprise.

insights.claim: Engineers found voids (air pockets) between carbon fiber layers in a newly cured forward propellant dome of Neutron's first stage, defects that could affect strength, durability and reliability.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Structural-margin discipline explains the delay and suggests Rocket Lab will not fly with known defects.
insights.quote: They don’t necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight

insights.claim: Neutron's first stage is the largest pressurized structure ever made from carbon composite, so Rocket Lab had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes and custom cure cycles for very large pieces like the domes.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Scale of the structure creates novel manufacturing risk that Rocket Lab cannot borrow from standard aerospace practice.
insights.quote: largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite

themes.theme: Root cause: design change after tank rupture

insights.claim: The voids trace to a design change that thickened some carbon composite sections, introduced after a Neutron propellant tank ruptured in a January hydrostatic pressure test because of a manufacturing defect at a critical join.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A fix for one failure created the next problem, showing iterative fixes may keep surfacing issues before flight.
insights.quote: Those thicker sections are where the voids formed

insights.claim: The failed tank was made by a third-party contractor using a manual hand-lay process to let tank testing proceed while Rocket Lab brought an automated fiber placement machine online, which is now operational; Rocket Lab also deleted joints in the first stage tank structure.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: In-house automated fiber placement should improve repeatability of future tank builds.
insights.locator: Officials said the failed carbon composite tank

insights.claim: Rocket Lab says the problem appears solved: an aft propellant dome made with the modified process passed inspection, and building a new forward dome plus investigation time pushed the launch to next year.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The fix is validated on one dome, so the forward dome result is the next proof point.

insights.claim: Final qualification of Neutron's first stage and of the methane-fueled Archimedes engine (nine power the booster) remain pending, after which a launch campaign in Virginia typically takes months, with integrated fueling tests, countdown rehearsals and a static fire that often reveal new problems.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Several gates remain, so 2027 is not safe from further slips.
insights.locator: Rocket Lab’s checklist for the first Neutron flight is long

insights.claim: Rocket Lab's stated strategy is to make orbit on the first try and avoid launching an unproven product, rather than learning on the first flight what could be learned in ground testing.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Quality-over-speed posture implies delays are preferred to a failed debut, which matters for reliability perception with customers.
insights.quote: Our aim is to make orbit on the first try

insights.claim: Neutron is 23 feet (7 meters) wide versus Electron's 3.9 feet, with lift capacity to low-Earth orbit near 29,000 pounds (13,000 kg), and Rocket Lab aims at US military and satellite megaconstellation customers; Electron has made 97 flights with 56 consecutive successes.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Electron success funds credibility; Neutron would widen the addressable launch market considerably.
insights.locator: The Neutron rocket is significantly larger

insights.claim: SpaceX is pivoting to Starship and will retire its workhorse Falcon 9 from commercial service in the next few years, which could open business for Rocket Lab from operators whose payloads do not suit Starship, but Relativity Space, Stoke Space and Firefly Aerospace are pursuing the same medium-lift market.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The medium-lift gap is a real opportunity but with a crowded field; first-to-fly matters.
